title: Division of Labor
objective: After this level you can explain Adam Smith's pin factory and why specializing raises output.
summary: In Adam Smith's pin factory (1776), ten workers splitting about 18 operations made upwards of 48,000 pins a day. Specializing builds skill, saves time and leads to machines.

cards.headline: One worker alone: perhaps not one pin a day. Ten together: 48,000.
cards.body: That's Adam Smith's famous pin factory, from the first chapter of The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776. Same people, same wire. The difference was how they split up the work.

cards.headline: Eighteen small jobs
cards.body: Smith counted about 18 distinct operations in making a pin. One worker draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, and so on down the line. Ten workers, each sticking to a few steps, could make upwards of 48,000 pins a day: about 4,800 each. Working alone, Smith reckoned, each could certainly not make 20, and perhaps not even one.

cards.headline: Why specializing works
cards.body: Smith gave three reasons. Practice: doing one task over and over makes you better at it. Time: nobody loses minutes switching from one kind of work to the next. Machines: dividing the work leads to machines that save labor. Same hands, far more pins.

cards.fact: Smith also saw the dark side of dividing labor.
cards.context: Later in the same book, he warned that a worker who spends a whole life on a few simple operations "generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become." Harsh words from the man who made the pin factory famous. Specializing multiplies output; it doesn't promise interesting work.

cards.headline: Division of labor: divided
learned: Smith's pin factory: 18 operations, 48,000 pins a day
Specializing builds skill and saves switching time
Dividing work leads to labor-saving machines
Smith warned endless repetition could dull minds

questions.prompt: In Smith's pin factory, about how many pins could ten specialized workers make in a day?

options.label: About 4,800
options.rationale: That's each worker's share; together they made upwards of 48,000.

questions.explanation: Ten workers dividing about 18 operations made upwards of 48,000 pins a day, about 4,800 each.

questions.prompt: What worried Smith about dividing work into tiny tasks?

options.label: Pins would become too cheap to sell
options.rationale: His worry was about workers, not pin prices.

options.label: Factories would need too many managers
options.rationale: That's Level 84's diseconomies of scale, not Smith's warning.

options.label: Workers would earn far too much
options.rationale: His warning was about minds, not pay.

questions.explanation: Smith warned that a lifetime of a few simple operations could leave a worker "as stupid and ignorant as it is possible" to become.

questions.prompt: Smith's pin workers and Level 72's Portugal and England gain in the same way. How?

options.label: Everyone does every step of the work themselves
options.rationale: That's the slow way: one worker alone made few pins.

options.label: Each specializes, and together they make more
Each buys machines from the other
options.rationale: The gain comes from splitting up the work.

options.label: The stronger side makes everything
options.rationale: Portugal gains by specializing, not by making both.

questions.explanation: Specializing raises total output, for pin workers and for trading countries alike.
